questions.prompt: An 'ad hoc' committee is one that is:
options: Formed for a particular purpose and usually temporary
questions.explanation: 'Ad hoc' (Latin, 'for this') means set up for a specific purpose, usually for a limited period.

questions.prompt: The appointment was made on an 'ad hoc' basis. This means the appointment is:
options: Temporary, made to meet an immediate need, pending regular selection
Permanent from the date of joining
Made by the President of India
questions.explanation: Ad hoc appointments are stop-gap arrangements until a regular appointment is made.

questions.prompt: The Assembly was adjourned 'sine die'. This means it was adjourned:
options: Without fixing a date for the next sitting
questions.explanation: 'Sine die' means 'without a day' – no date is fixed for reassembly. It is not dissolution.

questions.prompt: 'Prima facie' evidence means evidence that is:
options: Given by the first witness only
Sufficient at first sight, unless disproved
questions.explanation: 'Prima facie' means 'at first sight' or 'on the face of it'.

questions.prompt: The Collector found the complaint to be 'prima facie' true and ordered an inquiry. 'Prima facie' here means:
options: Proved beyond doubt after a trial
questions.explanation: An order of inquiry follows because the complaint appears true at first sight; full proof comes later.

questions.prompt: An action that is 'ultra vires' is one that is:
options: Beyond the legal powers of the authority taking it
Within the powers of the authority
questions.explanation: 'Ultra vires' (beyond the powers) describes acts exceeding legal authority; such acts are void.

questions.prompt: The opposite of 'ultra vires' is:
questions.explanation: 'Intra vires' means within the powers of the authority.

questions.prompt: A case heard 'in camera' is heard:
options: In private, with the public and press excluded
In the open court before the public
questions.explanation: 'In camera' (Latin, 'in a chamber') means in private.
questions.trick: In camera has nothing to do with cameras – think 'in chamber'.

questions.prompt: An 'interim' order is one that is:
options: The final judgment in a case
Temporary, in force until a final decision is made
Passed after the case is closed
An order that can never be modified
questions.explanation: 'Interim' means for the intervening period; an interim order holds until the final order.

questions.prompt: The term 'bona fide' means:
questions.explanation: 'Bona fide' means genuine or done in good faith; its opposite is 'mala fide'.

questions.prompt: An officer's action is described as 'mala fide'. This means the action was:
options: Done in bad faith, with a dishonest or improper motive
Done in the presence of a magistrate
questions.explanation: 'Mala fide' means in bad faith.

questions.prompt: 'Bona fide student certificate' is issued by an institution to certify that the person:
options: Has passed all examinations with distinction
Is a genuine student currently studying there
Is a former teacher of the institution
questions.explanation: A bona fide certificate confirms that the person is genuinely on the rolls of the institution.

questions.prompt: The Speaker 'pro tem' of a newly elected Assembly is:
options: The Speaker elected for five years
A temporary Speaker who presides until the regular Speaker is elected
The Governor's nominee for the Cabinet
questions.explanation: 'Pro tem' (pro tempore) means for the time being.

questions.prompt: 'Status quo' means:
questions.explanation: The court ordered 'status quo' – that is, things must remain as they are now.

questions.prompt: The court ordered both parties to maintain 'status quo' regarding the disputed land. This means:
options: The land must be sold immediately
The land goes to the government
Neither party should change the present position of the land until further orders
Both parties must build on the land
questions.explanation: Maintaining status quo means preserving the existing position.

questions.prompt: 'De facto' means:
options: In fact or in practice, whether or not legally recognised
questions.explanation: 'De facto' (in fact) contrasts with 'de jure' (by law).

questions.prompt: A ruler who holds power legally but not in practice is called the ruler:
questions.explanation: 'De jure' means by right or by law, as opposed to 'de facto' (in practice).

questions.prompt: The appointment was declared void 'ab initio'. This means it was void:
options: From the date of the court order only
For a period of one year
questions.explanation: 'Ab initio' means from the beginning; the appointment is treated as never valid.

questions.prompt: The phrase 'inter alia' in an official order means:
questions.explanation: 'Inter alia' indicates that only some items are being mentioned from a larger list.

questions.prompt: Bonus was distributed 'pro rata' among the employees. This means it was distributed:
options: In proportion to each employee's share (e.g., service or salary)
As a free gift to the public
questions.explanation: 'Pro rata' means proportionately.

questions.prompt: 'Mutatis mutandis' in a Government Order means that the rules apply:
options: With the necessary changes having been made
questions.explanation: Mutatis mutandis = 'the necessary changes having been made'.

questions.prompt: 'Ipso facto' means:
questions.explanation: E.g., a person convicted of certain offences is ipso facto disqualified – automatically, by that very fact.

questions.prompt: The proposal was rejected 'in toto'. This means it was rejected:
questions.explanation: 'In toto' means entirely.

questions.prompt: A person who has 'locus standi' in a case has:
options: The right to be heard in that court or proceeding
questions.explanation: Locus standi is the legal standing to bring an action or be heard.

questions.prompt: A matter that is 'sub judice' is one that:
options: Can be freely debated in the Assembly
Is under consideration by a court and not yet decided
questions.explanation: Matters pending before a court are sub judice and are generally not discussed in the legislature.

questions.prompt: An 'ex gratia' payment made by the Government to the family of a victim is:
options: Made as a gesture of goodwill, not as a legal obligation
A fine imposed on the family
A salary arrear due by law
questions.explanation: 'Ex gratia' means 'out of grace'; it is not legally owed.

questions.prompt: An 'ex parte' order is passed:
options: In the absence of, or without hearing, the other party
questions.explanation: Ex parte = on behalf of one side only.

questions.prompt: The Chief Secretary is a member of the board 'ex officio'. This means he is a member:
options: Because of the office he holds
questions.explanation: Ex officio membership comes automatically with holding a particular post.

questions.prompt: The High Court took up the issue of potholes on city roads 'suo motu' on the basis of a newspaper report. This means the Court:
options: Transferred the case to the Supreme Court
Waited for the Government to file a case
Took up the case on its own, without a petition being filed
questions.explanation: Suo motu = on its own motion.

questions.prompt: If a meeting is adjourned for 'want of quorum', it means:
options: The minimum number of members needed to transact business were not present
The chairman was absent on leave
The members disagreed on every point
questions.explanation: Quorum is the minimum attendance required for valid proceedings; without it, the meeting cannot proceed.

questions.prompt: 'Quid pro quo' means:
options: Something given in return for something else
questions.explanation: It refers to an exchange of favours.

questions.prompt: 'Persona non grata' refers to a person who is:
options: Not welcome or not acceptable, especially a diplomat asked to leave a country
A person who has no nationality
questions.explanation: A host country may declare a foreign diplomat persona non grata.

questions.prompt: 'Vice versa' means:
questions.explanation: E.g., 'Officers must inform staff of changes, and vice versa' – staff must also inform officers.

questions.prompt: The abbreviation 'viz.' in an official letter means:
questions.explanation: 'Viz.' (videlicet) introduces a full list: 'three districts, viz., Salem, Erode and Namakkal'.
questions.trick: viz. = namely (full list); e.g. = for example (part list).

questions.prompt: 'N.B.' written in a circular stands for 'Nota bene', which means:
questions.explanation: N.B. draws the reader's attention to an important point.

questions.prompt: 'Per se' means:
questions.explanation: E.g., 'Delay per se is not a ground for rejection' – delay by itself is not enough.

questions.prompt: A 'caveat' filed in a court is:
options: A request to transfer a judge
A notice requesting that no order be passed in a matter without first hearing the person who filed it
questions.explanation: A caveat (Latin, 'let him beware') ensures the caveator is heard before any order is passed.

questions.prompt: The witness's statement was recorded 'verbatim'. This means it was recorded:
options: Word for word, exactly as spoken
questions.explanation: Verbatim = in exactly the same words.

questions.prompt: A 'viva voce' examination is:
options: A practical examination in a laboratory
questions.explanation: Viva voce = 'by the living voice', i.e., oral.

questions.prompt: The writ of 'Habeas Corpus' is issued to:
options: Produce a detained person before the court to examine whether the detention is lawful
Command a public official to perform a duty
Question a person's right to hold a public office
Transfer a case from a lower court
questions.explanation: Habeas corpus ('you may have the body') protects personal liberty against unlawful detention.

questions.prompt: The writ of 'Mandamus' is a command issued by a court to:
options: Release a person from illegal detention
Stop a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction
Remove a person illegally holding a public office
A public authority to perform a public duty it has failed to perform
questions.explanation: Mandamus means 'we command'.

questions.prompt: The writ of 'Quo Warranto' asks a person:
options: By what authority he holds a public office
Why he has not paid tax
Why a lower court's record should not be quashed
questions.explanation: Quo warranto ('by what warrant') challenges the right to hold a public office.

questions.prompt: Which writ is issued by a higher court to quash the order of a lower court or tribunal that acted without jurisdiction?
questions.explanation: Certiorari ('to be certified') quashes orders already passed; Prohibition prevents a lower court from proceeding further.
questions.trick: Prohibition stops a case midway; certiorari quashes an order already made.

questions.prompt: An 'affidavit' is:
options: A written statement confirmed by oath or affirmation before an authorised officer
questions.explanation: Affidavits are sworn before a notary or other authorised official and can be used as evidence.

questions.prompt: A 'corrigendum' issued by an office is:
options: A notice correcting an error in an earlier order or publication
questions.explanation: Corrigendum = something to be corrected.

questions.prompt: An 'addendum' to a Government Order is:
options: Something added to it as a supplement
questions.explanation: An addendum adds material to an earlier document without changing the rest.

questions.prompt: A 'moratorium' on loan repayment means:
options: A temporary suspension or postponement of repayment
questions.explanation: Moratorium = authorised delay or suspension of an activity or obligation for a period.

questions.prompt: An 'embargo' is:
options: An official ban, especially on trade with a country
questions.explanation: An embargo prohibits trade or other activity by official order.

questions.prompt: A 'Notification' issued by the Government is usually:
options: A private letter to an officer
A note written on a file
Published in the Gazette to announce rules, appointments or orders having legal effect
questions.explanation: Statutory rules, appointments of gazetted officers, etc., are notified in the Gazette.

questions.prompt: A 'Circular' is a communication that is:
options: Written by a citizen to the Collector
Sent to several offices or officers at once, conveying instructions or information
questions.explanation: Circulars circulate the same message to many recipients.

questions.prompt: An 'Ordinance' in a State is promulgated by:
options: The Chief Justice of the High Court
The Governor, when the Legislative Assembly is not in session
questions.explanation: Under Article 213, the Governor may promulgate ordinances when the Legislature is not in session; they have the force of law.

questions.prompt: An 'Ordinance' issued by the Governor must be laid before the State Legislature and ceases to operate at the expiration of:
options: Six weeks from the reassembly of the Legislature, unless approved earlier
questions.explanation: Article 213(2): an ordinance ceases six weeks after the Legislature reassembles, unless disapproved earlier.

questions.prompt: The term 'Minutes' of a meeting refers to:
options: The time limit for each speaker
The list of items to be discussed
The official written record of the proceedings and decisions of a meeting
questions.explanation: Minutes record what was discussed and decided; the agenda lists what will be discussed.

questions.prompt: A 'Resolution' passed in a meeting is:
options: A formal decision taken by the members
questions.explanation: Resolutions record formal decisions adopted by a meeting.

questions.prompt: A 'Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)' between the Government and a company is:
options: A written document recording the agreed intentions of the parties
questions.explanation: An MoU records the broad terms on which parties agree to cooperate.

questions.prompt: A 'press release' issued by a Government department is meant for:
options: Giving official information to the media for publication
questions.explanation: Press releases communicate official news to the public through the media.

questions.prompt: 'Delegation of powers' in administration means:
options: A higher authority entrusting some of its powers to a subordinate authority
questions.explanation: Delegation helps quicker decisions at lower levels, while ultimate responsibility remains with the delegating authority.

questions.prompt: 'Ex post facto' sanction for an expenditure means sanction given:
options: After the expenditure has already been incurred
questions.explanation: Ex post facto = after the fact; it regularises action already taken.

questions.prompt: A decision 'in principle' means:
options: The proposal is implemented immediately in full
The decision applies only to principals of schools
The proposal is accepted in general, with details to be worked out later
questions.explanation: Approval in principle is approval of the basic idea, subject to final details and formal sanction.

questions.prompt: 'Res judicata' means that:
options: Every case must be heard twice
A judge can reopen any case at will
A matter already finally decided by a competent court cannot be tried again between the same parties
Cases are decided by the public
questions.explanation: Res judicata ('a matter judged') bars re-litigation of the same issue.

questions.prompt: 'Superannuation' of a government servant refers to:
options: Retirement on attaining the age prescribed in the service rules
questions.explanation: Retirement on reaching the prescribed age is retirement on superannuation.

questions.prompt: In service rules, 'lien' means:
options: The right of a government servant to hold a regular post substantively, to which he can return
questions.explanation: An employee on deputation retains a lien on his parent post and returns to it later.

questions.prompt: 'Probation' in government service refers to:
options: A period of leave without pay
A period of trial after appointment, during which the employee's suitability is assessed
questions.explanation: On satisfactory completion of probation, the employee is declared an approved probationer.

questions.prompt: An officer is said to be 'officiating' in a post when he:
options: Performs the duties of a post on which another person holds a lien, or a vacant post, without holding it substantively
Has been dismissed from that post
Is on long leave from that post
questions.explanation: Officiating means discharging the duties of a post temporarily, not as its substantive holder.

questions.prompt: 'Full Additional Charge' (FAC) of a post means an officer:
options: Is relieved of all his duties
Is promoted permanently to a higher post
Gets double pay without extra work
Holds the full charge of another post in addition to his own regular post
questions.explanation: When a post is vacant, an officer may be asked to hold its full additional charge besides his own.

questions.prompt: A government servant placed under 'suspension' is:
options: Temporarily kept away from duty, pending an inquiry or criminal case
questions.explanation: Suspension is not a penalty by itself; the employee remains in service but cannot perform duties.

questions.prompt: The allowance paid to a government servant during the period of suspension is called:
questions.explanation: A suspended employee gets subsistence allowance instead of full pay.

questions.prompt: 'Reversion' of a government servant means:
options: Sending him back from a higher post to a lower post
questions.explanation: Reversion returns an officiating or promoted employee to his lower (substantive) post.

questions.prompt: 'Voluntary retirement' means:
options: Retirement at the employee's own request before the age of superannuation, as allowed by rules
Retirement on reaching the prescribed age
Retirement because of the post being abolished
questions.explanation: Voluntary retirement is sought by the employee; compulsory retirement is ordered by the Government.

questions.prompt: A 'Charge Memo' issued to a government servant:
options: Sets out the charges of misconduct against him and calls for his explanation
questions.explanation: Disciplinary proceedings start with a memo of charges; the employee is given an opportunity to reply.

questions.prompt: Under the Tamil Nadu Civil Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, a charge memo under Rule 17(b) relates to:
questions.explanation: Rule 17(a) proceedings are for minor penalties; Rule 17(b) proceedings are for major penalties such as removal or dismissal.

questions.prompt: 'Censure' in disciplinary matters is:
options: A formal written reprimand recorded against an employee
questions.explanation: Censure is one of the lightest formal penalties.

questions.prompt: An 'annual increment' is:
options: The yearly rise in pay within the scale of pay of a post
questions.explanation: Increments move the employee to the next stage of the pay scale each year.

questions.prompt: 'Stoppage of increment' as a penalty means:
options: The employee's yearly rise in pay is withheld for a specified period
questions.explanation: Withholding of increment is a penalty that delays the employee's pay rise.

questions.prompt: 'Dearness Allowance' (DA) is paid to government employees to:
options: Compensate for the rise in the cost of living
Meet the cost of house rent
questions.explanation: DA is revised periodically in line with price indices to neutralise inflation.

questions.prompt: 'House Rent Allowance' (HRA) is admissible to an employee who:
options: Lives in a government quarters rent-free
Does not occupy government-provided accommodation, as per the rules
Is on leave without pay for a year
questions.explanation: HRA helps employees meet rent when they do not live in government quarters.

questions.prompt: The 'Daily Allowance' (DA) paid on tour is meant to cover:
options: The extra expenses of an employee while camping away from headquarters on duty
The cost of living at the headquarters
questions.explanation: On tour, Daily Allowance meets boarding and incidental expenses away from headquarters (not to be confused with Dearness Allowance).

questions.prompt: 'Earned Leave' is so called because:
options: It is granted only on medical grounds
It is earned by the employee in proportion to the period spent on duty
It is a reward for promotion
It is given only to retired employees
questions.explanation: Earned leave accrues with duty and can be accumulated within limits.

questions.prompt: 'Loss of Pay' (LOP) leave means:
options: Leave for which no pay or allowances are paid
questions.explanation: When no other leave is admissible, absence may be treated as leave on loss of pay.

questions.prompt: 'Casual Leave' is meant for:
options: Higher studies abroad for two years
Short absences for unforeseen or personal reasons
questions.explanation: Casual leave covers brief absences; it is not regular leave earned by duty.

questions.prompt: A 'No Objection Certificate' (NOC) is issued by an authority to state that:
options: The applicant has committed an offence
The applicant must pay a fine
It has no objection to the proposed action of the applicant
questions.explanation: E.g., a department issues an NOC before an employee applies for another job or a passport.

questions.prompt: A 'relieving order' is issued when an employee:
options: Joins service for the first time
Is released from his present post, e.g., on transfer or retirement
questions.explanation: The relieving order formally ends his duties in the old post; he then submits a joining report at the new one.

questions.prompt: 'Joining time' refers to:
options: The time of reporting to office every day
The time allowed to a transferred employee to join the new post
The time allowed to reply to a charge memo
questions.explanation: Joining time allows for travel and settling between relief from the old post and joining the new one.

questions.prompt: The 'Service Register' of a government employee contains:
options: A record of the employee's entire service history, such as appointment, pay, leave and promotions
The daily attendance of all staff
questions.explanation: The Service Register (Service Book) is the authoritative record of an employee's service.

questions.prompt: An 'Annual Confidential Report' (ACR) records:
options: An assessment of an employee's work and conduct during the year
The annual budget of the department
questions.explanation: ACRs are used for assessing suitability for promotion and confirmation.

questions.prompt: A 'Panel' prepared for promotion is:
options: A wooden board in the office
An approved list of eligible persons, in order, for promotion to a higher post
questions.explanation: A promotion panel lists those found fit, usually in order of seniority/merit.

questions.prompt: 'Regularisation' of service means:
options: Bringing a temporary or ad hoc appointee into regular service in accordance with rules
questions.explanation: Regularisation converts irregular or temporary service into regular service.

questions.prompt: A 'compassionate appointment' is made to:
options: A dependant of a government servant who died in harness, to relieve the family's financial distress
An employee who has been promoted twice
A retired officer for a second term
A candidate who topped the competitive examination
questions.explanation: Compassionate appointment helps the bereaved family of an employee who died while in service.

questions.prompt: 'Sanctioned strength' of an office refers to:
options: The number of employees present today
The physical fitness of the staff
The number of posts approved by the Government for that office
questions.explanation: Sanctioned strength is the total of posts sanctioned, whether filled or vacant.

questions.prompt: The 'Cadre strength' minus the 'number of persons in position' gives the number of:
questions.explanation: Vacant posts = sanctioned posts not presently filled.

questions.prompt: A 'Gazetted Officer' is so called because:
options: He reads the Gazette every day
His appointment is notified in the Government Gazette
He is appointed by a private company
questions.explanation: Appointments of gazetted officers are published in the official Gazette; they are authorised to attest documents.

questions.prompt: 'Attestation' of a copy of a certificate by a gazetted officer means:
options: Certifying that the copy is a true copy of the original
questions.explanation: The officer compares the copy with the original and certifies it as a true copy.

questions.prompt: 'Commutation of pension' means:
options: Receiving a lump sum in exchange for giving up a portion of the monthly pension
Transferring the pension to another person
questions.explanation: A pensioner may commute (convert) part of the pension into an immediate lump-sum payment.

questions.prompt: 'Gratuity' paid to a retiring government servant is:
options: A lump-sum payment in recognition of long service
questions.explanation: Gratuity is a one-time retirement benefit related to length of service.

questions.prompt: 'Family pension' is paid to:
options: The eligible family members of a deceased government servant or pensioner
questions.explanation: Family pension supports the family after the employee's or pensioner's death.

questions.prompt: 'Re-appropriation' in government finance means:
options: Transfer of savings from one unit of appropriation to meet excess expenditure under another, within the same grant
questions.explanation: Re-appropriation shifts funds between heads within the same grant, with sanction of the competent authority.

questions.prompt: A 'Supplementary Grant' is sought from the Legislature when:
options: The amount authorised for a service in the current year is found insufficient
questions.explanation: Under Article 205, supplementary grants are presented when sanctioned funds are insufficient.

questions.prompt: A 'Vote on Account' allows the Government to:
options: Collect new taxes without a law
Withdraw money for expenditure for part of the year pending the passing of the full budget
questions.explanation: Vote on account grants advance approval for expenditure for a part of the financial year.

questions.prompt: The financial year of the Government of Tamil Nadu runs from:
questions.explanation: Government accounts in India follow the April–March financial year.

questions.prompt: An 'Imprest' (permanent advance) is:
options: The annual salary of an officer
A fixed sum kept with an officer to meet petty and urgent expenses, recouped periodically
questions.explanation: Imprest money is replenished on presentation of accounts for the amount spent.

questions.prompt: 'Contingent expenditure' in an office refers to:
options: Expenditure on incidental items such as stationery, postage and minor repairs
questions.explanation: Contingencies are the incidental charges of running an office.

questions.prompt: An 'honorarium' is:
options: A monthly salary for regular work
A payment made for occasional or special work that is not part of one's regular duties
questions.explanation: E.g., an honorarium may be paid to an employee for setting question papers.

questions.prompt: 'Arrears' of pay means:
options: Advance pay for the next month
Amounts that were due earlier but have not yet been paid
questions.explanation: Pay revisions with retrospective effect often result in arrears.

questions.prompt: A 'Tender' in government purchase is:
options: A formal offer by a supplier or contractor to supply goods or do work at a stated price
questions.explanation: Government invites tenders to obtain competitive prices.

questions.prompt: 'Earnest Money Deposit' (EMD) is collected from tenderers to:
options: Pay the salaries of the tender committee
Ensure that bidders are serious and do not withdraw their offers
Refund the cost of the tender form
questions.explanation: EMD is a security deposit forfeited if a bidder backs out; it is refunded to unsuccessful bidders.

questions.prompt: An 'Indent' in an office is:
options: A formal requisition or order for supplies
questions.explanation: Offices place indents for stationery, forms or stores.

questions.prompt: A 'Challan' is used to:
options: Remit money into the Government account at the treasury or bank
questions.explanation: Challans accompany payments of fees, taxes and dues into the Government account.

questions.prompt: An 'audit objection' (audit para) is raised when:
options: Auditors find an irregularity or lack of proper sanction in accounts
questions.explanation: Audit objections must be answered and settled by the department concerned.

questions.prompt: In Tamil Nadu's revenue administration, a 'Patta' is:
options: A revenue record establishing the ownership and right over a piece of land
questions.explanation: Patta is issued by the Revenue Department in the name of the landholder, showing survey number and extent.

questions.prompt: 'Adangal' in Tamil Nadu village accounts is:
options: The register maintained by the Village Administrative Officer showing details of land and the crops cultivated
A register of births and deaths only
questions.explanation: Adangal records cultivation details for each survey number in the village.

questions.prompt: An 'Encumbrance Certificate' (EC) shows:
options: The income of the property owner
The caste of the property owner
The registered transactions and liabilities relating to a property over a period
The electricity consumption of the property
questions.explanation: ECs are issued by the Registration Department and are used to check if a property is free of encumbrances.

questions.prompt: In Tamil Nadu, a 'Firka' is:
options: A revenue unit consisting of a group of villages within a taluk, under a Revenue Inspector
questions.explanation: Revenue hierarchy: district – division – taluk – firka – village.

questions.prompt: 'Jamabandi' in Tamil Nadu revenue administration refers to:
options: The annual inspection and settlement of village revenue accounts
questions.explanation: Jamabandi is the annual audit of village accounts conducted by revenue officers.

questions.prompt: The officer in charge of a Taluk in Tamil Nadu is the:
questions.explanation: The Tahsildar heads the taluk; the RDO heads a revenue division; the Collector heads the district.

questions.prompt: In Tamil Nadu Government usage, 'G.O.' stands for:
questions.explanation: A G.O. is the formal order by which the State Government conveys its decisions.

questions.prompt: A Tamil Nadu Government Order is numbered 'G.O.(Ms) No. 45'. In this series name, 'Ms' denotes:
questions.explanation: G.O.(Ms) – Manuscript series – is used for orders of general importance, such as policy decisions and rules.

questions.prompt: Leave sanctioned to a single Secretariat assistant was issued as 'G.O.(Rt) No. 210'. What does 'Rt' mean?
questions.explanation: G.O.(Rt) – Routine series – covers routine matters such as individual leave, transfers or minor sanctions.

questions.prompt: Which type of Government Order would normally be used to issue a new State policy affecting the public at large?
questions.explanation: Policy decisions and orders of general importance are issued as G.O.(Ms); routine individual matters as G.O.(Rt).

questions.prompt: A 'D.O. letter' is a:
questions.explanation: D.O. = Demi-Official; it is written in a personal form from one officer to another.

questions.prompt: A Demi-Official (D.O.) letter is used when an officer wishes to:
options: Draw the personal attention of another officer to a matter, in a personal and friendly tone
Order the arrest of a person
questions.explanation: D.O. letters are written in the first person to secure personal attention or exchange views informally.

questions.prompt: A Demi-Official letter usually ends with the complimentary close:
questions.explanation: As a personal form of official correspondence, a D.O. letter begins 'Dear Thiru/Tmt. ...' and ends 'Yours sincerely'.

questions.prompt: A 'U.O. note' stands for:
questions.explanation: U.O. = Unofficial.

questions.prompt: An 'Unofficial (U.O.) note' is mainly used for:
options: Consultation or exchange of views between departments or offices of the same Government
questions.explanation: U.O. notes are used for inter-departmental consultation and do not carry a salutation or complimentary close.

questions.prompt: A 'Memorandum' as a form of official communication is written:
options: In the first person with 'Dear Sir'
In the third person, without a salutation or complimentary close
questions.explanation: A memorandum (memo) is signed with the officer's designation and has no salutation or closing.

questions.prompt: An 'Endorsement' in official correspondence is used to:
options: Fix the salary of an employee
Forward a copy of a communication to another office for information or action
questions.explanation: An endorsement (e.g., 'Copy forwarded to ...') sends copies or returns papers without a separate covering letter.

questions.prompt: In Tamil Nadu, orders issued by Heads of Departments and District Collectors are commonly issued in the form of:
questions.explanation: E.g., 'Proceedings of the District Collector, Madurai' or 'Proceedings of the Director of School Education'.

questions.prompt: An 'Office Order' is generally used for:
options: Internal administrative matters of an office, such as distribution of work or sanction of leave
questions.explanation: Office orders deal with the internal working of an office.
